title: Experience Systems
category: UX from basics to complex workflows
summary: How design tokens, component libraries, accessibility baselines, and domain workflows stay coherent—from marketing clarity to offline-capable operational software and human-controlled AI flows.
role: Principal UI engineer — design systems, interaction models, accessibility, and complex product UX
timeframe: Design-system packages, consulting-site baselines, show-operations MVP, and portfolio UX surfaces, 2019–2026
problem: Teams ship both simple public journeys and dense internal tools. Without a shared grammar for state, recovery, and accessibility, basic pages drift and complex workflows become unteachable.
constraints: Client and employer design systems remain referenced only at the pattern level; proprietary tokens and brand kits stay out of public copy.
Basic marketing UX must meet WCAG-minded baselines (skip links, landmarks, focus, and reduced motion) without waiting for a redesign.
Complex domains—show hierarchies, dependencies, offline queues, and approval gates—need typed models and reversible actions, not only prettier screens.
Proof surfaces (kitchen sinks, Storybook, and axe/Playwright checks) have to travel with the system so quality is inspectable.
approach: Anchor basic UX in tokens, constrained component sets, and content-driven pages so marketing and admin previews share one visual language.
Raise the floor with accessibility as architecture: route announcers, skip links, forced-colors awareness, and automated axe coverage where the stack allows.
Model complex UX as domain contracts—workspace → show → segment → entry, with lock, version, dependency, and impact—before decorating the UI.
Design recovery and offline paths as visible states (queue, conflict, retry) rather than silent background magic.
Keep human approval in agentic flows: interpreted goals, bounded plans, and explicit approve/reject before irreversible work.
Expose the system through /styles kitchen-sink lanes, Storybook libraries, and decision journals so hiring teams can inspect the grammar.
